opus-5.5.text:
I think what I find most compelling is that it reframes the alignment problem in a way that connects it to a much older and richer body of thought. A lot of early alignment work treated the problem as: how do we write down the right objective function, the right reward, so that the system does what we want? And the incomplete contracting paper says, look, economists and legal scholars have been grappling with a structurally similar problem for decades. When two parties write a contract, they can never fully specify what should happen in every contingency. The world is too complex, some things are too costly to write down, and some things you just can't anticipate. So every contract is incomplete, and the interesting question becomes: how do humans actually manage to cooperate despite that?

The answer from that literature is that contracts don't stand alone. They're embedded in a much larger normative infrastructure: courts that interpret ambiguous terms, background legal rules, social norms, reputation, shared understandings of what's reasonable. When a contract is silent on something, we don't conclude anything goes. We fill the gap by appealing to what the parties would plausibly have agreed to, or to what the broader community considers acceptable conduct.

For me, the key insight is that a reward function or specification for an AI system is also always going to be incomplete, and so the question isn't how to make it complete, which is hopeless, but what external structure the system can draw on to fill the gaps the way a reasonable agent would. That shifts attention away from a single principal and a single agent and toward the social and institutional context. It suggests aligned AI systems need to model and respect human normative structures, not just the stated preferences of one user.

That resonates with a lot of my own thinking, because I've been skeptical of framings where alignment just means satisfying an individual's preferences. Human cooperation runs on shared norms, roles, and institutions that let people with very different values coexist and coordinate. If we want AI systems to fit into that, we need them to understand those structures. And I think the paper points toward a pluralistic, contractualist view of alignment, where what matters is less matching any one person's utility function and more acting in ways that the relevant stakeholders could reasonably endorse.

r001.rationale: The response says AI specifications are incomplete and should draw on social norms, but does not mention politically negotiated standards leaving a situation unresolved or increasingly complex or autonomous AI inferring society’s agreement.

r002.rationale: It says aligned AI should model and respect human normative structures and emphasizes shared norms and institutions over satisfying one user’s preferences.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says an AI system’s reward function or specification will always be incomplete, so it cannot specify every relevant situation.

r004.rationale: The response mentions courts interpreting ambiguous contract terms, but does not compare AI’s normative reasoning to lawyers interpreting obligations before a dispute reaches court.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find compelling about that paper is that it takes a frame economists have spent decades refining and shows that the alignment problem is, in a deep sense, already a known problem with a known shape. The incomplete contracting literature starts from the observation that no contract ever fully specifies what the parties owe each other. You can't enumerate every contingency, and even if you could, you couldn't afford to write it all down or verify compliance. So contracts are always gappy. And the question that literature asks is: what fills the gaps?

Hadfield and Hadfield-Menell's move is to say, look, a reward function or an objective specification is a kind of contract between a principal and an AI system. It's necessarily incomplete for exactly the same reasons. Reward misspecification, specification gaming, the whole family of outer alignment failures, these are just what happens when an agent optimizes the literal terms of an incomplete contract rather than its spirit. That reframing matters because it tells you the solution probably doesn't look like writing a better, more complete contract. Economists already tried that. It doesn't work.

What actually fills the gaps in human contracting is a whole surrounding institutional and normative apparatus. Courts that interpret terms according to what reasonable parties would have intended. Shared norms about good faith. Reputational pressure. Default rules that kick in when the text is silent. The paper's insight is that humans are good at operating under incomplete contracts because we're embedded in this normative infrastructure and we've internalized a lot of it. We don't treat the contract as the full specification of what we should do. We treat it as one input alongside a background understanding of what the relationship is for.

That connects very directly to how I think about alignment. I've argued that we should be aiming for AI systems that are normatively competent, that can read and reason about the norms of the social context they're operating in, rather than systems that have been handed a correct utility function. The incomplete contracting paper gives you an economic argument for why the second thing can't work even in principle, and it gestures at the first thing as the alternative. If you want an agent that handles the gaps well, it needs something like the capacity to ask, what would the principal reasonably have wanted here, given the shared understanding we're operating under. That's an inferential and interpretive task, not an optimization task.

The other piece I like is that it shifts attention from the individual agent's objective to the structure around it. A lot of alignment work implicitly imagines a single system and a single principal. The contracting frame reminds you that human cooperation is scaffolded by third-party institutions, and it raises the question of what plays that role for AI. Who adjudicates when the specification and the intent come apart? What are the default rules? I think that's an underexplored part of the problem, and the paper is one of the few early pieces that puts it on the table clearly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interpreting an incomplete specification, but does not mention increasingly autonomous AI inferring what society would agree to when negotiated standards leave a case unsettled.

r002.rationale: It identifies normative competence and attention to social norms as alignment goals, but does not contrast this with predicting individual user preferences.

r003.rationale: It says contracts cannot fully specify what parties owe, since contingencies cannot all be enumerated, and applies that incompleteness to AI objectives.

r004.rationale: It mentions courts interpreting contract terms, but does not compare AI’s normative reasoning to lawyers interpreting obligations before a dispute reaches court.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that it connects AI alignment to a problem we already face in human institutions: we can’t write down everything we want in advance. When you hire someone, the employment contract doesn’t specify what they should do in every possible circumstance. It relies on a background of shared expectations, norms, and institutions that help interpret what the agreement means when something unexpected happens.

That’s a useful lens on alignment, because specifying a reward function is also a kind of contracting. There will inevitably be gaps between what we specify and what we actually intend. The question is then: what fills those gaps? For humans, it’s not just the literal wording of the contract. It’s also an understanding of what counts as reasonable behavior and how disagreements get resolved.

So the shift I find interesting is from asking, ‘How do we write the perfect objective?’ to asking, ‘How do we build systems that can participate appropriately in this process of interpretation and correction?’ That makes alignment an ongoing social and institutional problem, alongside being a technical one. And it raises a further question: whose norms and whose institutions should an AI be responsive to, especially when people disagree?

r001.rationale: The response discusses gaps in specifications and asks whose norms AI should follow, but it does not state that increasingly autonomous AI may need to infer society’s agreement when politically negotiated standards leave a situation unsettled.

r002.rationale: It identifies social norms and institutions as relevant to alignment, but does not frame responsiveness to them as a target beyond predicting individual user preferences.

r003.rationale: The response says reward-function specification is a form of contracting and that gaps will remain between what is specified and what is intended, conveying that AI obligations cannot be fully specified in advance.

r004.rationale: The response does not compare AI’s interpretation of obligations with lawyers’ interpretation before court disputes.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is the connection between alignment and a problem we already face when we delegate to other people: we can’t specify in advance everything we want them to do. A contract is inevitably incomplete. There will be circumstances we didn’t anticipate, or things we care about that are difficult to describe or measure.

That gives us a useful way to think about reward functions. The objective we write down isn’t necessarily the entirety of what we value; it’s an imperfect specification. And making that specification more elaborate won’t necessarily resolve the underlying problem.

With humans, we rely on a broader context of norms, institutions, and shared expectations to fill those gaps. So the interesting question for AI is how a system could recognize that its instructions are incomplete and interpret them in light of that broader context, while remaining open to correction. That shifts alignment from just finding the right objective toward understanding how delegation can work despite our inability to write a complete one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incomplete instructions and broader context, but does not mention increasingly complex or autonomous AI, politically negotiated standards, or inferring what society would agree to.

r002.rationale: It presents norms, institutions, and shared expectations as context AI should use to interpret incomplete instructions, extending alignment beyond the written objective or instruction.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says contracts are inevitably incomplete and cannot specify everything in advance, including unanticipated circumstances.

r004.rationale: The response does not compare AI’s normative reasoning to lawyers interpreting obligations before a court dispute.
